newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Thai, Vietnam rice markets unswayed by Deng death.
newsitem.headline: Thai, Vietnam rice markets unswayed by Deng death.

text.p: Rice markets in Thailand and Vietnam stayed dull on Thursday showing little reaction to news of the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
Dealers in both Ho Chi Minh City and Bangkok said attention was focused on other factors. Consequently prices were either slightly lower or unchanged.
"What makes the market boil this week was not Deng's death, but rather the report that China had recently slapped import duty on Thai fragrant rice," said a trader from a major rice firm in Bangkok.
"China is a big market for high quality rice. With our competitiveness being crippled there and market share of lower-quality being bitten into, we could be in trouble," he added.
Thai benchmark 100 percent B grade was quoted at $360-390 per tonne FOB Bangkok from $370-390 last week while 100 percent fragrant rice was barely changed at $620-630 per tonne.

In Ho Chi Minh City, where news of Deng's death was only announced at midday, traders said prices had remained steady from last week with five percent broken quoted at around $270 per tonne and 10 percent broken at $265.
"There've been a lot of foreign buyers coming to have a look at the market," said a Ho Chi Minh City dealer during afternoon trade. "But it's not affected us much."
He added that a more significant factor for the market was news earlier this week of a deal between Vietnam and the Philippines to purchase up to 200,000 tonnes of rice.
"We're hearing also that the trade ministry may try to impose a $280 per tonne minimum price next week, so there are other factors around" one said. "It's better to wait a bit and see."
China imported 631,180 tonnes of rice from Thailand in 1996 some 465,092 tonnes of which were fragrant rice.
Official confirmation of the tariff report was not available.
Trade sources in Bangkok said they did not expect Deng's death to have any short-term impact in the rice market.
"It is something that has been factored in the market for almost two years. I think the powers-that-be there have already made a decision on who will succeed him," said another trader.
Traders expected prices to ease slightly next week if demand remains thin.
"But it also depends on supplies. If the supplies entering the market continue to be limited, the prices might remain at this level, if not higher" he said.
